text_blocks.snippet: CPR in the elderly carries significant risks due to their often fragile state and pre-existing health conditions. While CPR can be life-saving, it can also lead to serious injuries and poor outcomes in older adults. Common risks include rib and sternum fractures, neurological damage, and internal organ injuries.
snippet_highlighted_words: rib and sternum fractures, neurological damage, and internal organ injuries

list.title: Rib and sternum fractures:
list.snippet: The force required for chest compressions can easily fracture ribs and the sternum, especially in older adults with decreased bone density.

list.title: Other injuries:
list.snippet: CPR can also cause bruising, lung damage, internal bleeding, and damage to the trachea or esophagus.

list.title: Organ damage:
list.snippet: In rare cases, CPR can lead to liver lacerations or stomach rupture.

list.title: Neurological damage:
list.snippet: Lack of oxygen during cardiac arrest can lead to brain damage, and the process of CPR itself can exacerbate this.

list.title: Low survival rates:
list.snippet: Survival rates for CPR in the elderly, especially those with chronic illnesses, are generally low.

list.title: Quality of life:
list.snippet: Even if CPR is successful, the older adult may not return to their previous level of function and may experience a poor quality of life.

list.title: Prolonged dying process:
list.snippet: In some cases, CPR can prolong the dying process, adding to the patient's suffering without a meaningful chance of recovery.

list.title: Emotional impact on family and caregivers:
list.snippet: Families may experience emotional distress, financial burdens, and the psychological impact of supporting a disabled survivor.

list.title: Moral distress for medical providers:
list.snippet: Medical professionals may experience moral distress and burnout from performing CPR that is unlikely to be successful in elderly patients.
